mainTopic: Vows on foods and on clothing, mushrooms and their ברכה, and רבי יהודה's rule that a vow follows the vower's situation
overview: This amud opens with the last line of the story about רבא and רב יוסף, a פסוק showing that a humble person is lifted up. Then a ברייתא explains what is included when someone vows off דגן (grain), 'produce of the year,' or 'produce of the land.' It says mushrooms count as 'growths of the ground' but not 'produce of the land.' The גמרא asks how this fits with the ברכה rule that mushrooms get שהכל because they do not grow from the ground. אביי answers that mushrooms grow from the earth but feed from the air, and the משנה in ברכות is read to match. Next comes a new משנה: a vow against clothing does not include sackcloth or sheets, and a vow against wool or flax does not include raw fleece or raw flax. רבי יהודה adds that everything follows the vower's situation. The גמרא brings ברייתות that list items that do count as clothing, discuss going out on שבת in rain coverings, and give examples of רבי יהודה's rule with wool and flax.

steps.title: The verse that closes the story of humility
steps.stepSummary: The previous story ends with the פסוק 'Every valley shall be lifted,' showing that one who lowers himself is raised up.
steps.simpleTranslation: As it is said: 'Every valley shall be lifted up.'
steps.whatsHappening: This is the last line of the story from the previous section. It gives the פסוק that backs up רבא's teaching that a humble person gets lifted up.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A valley is the lowest place, yet the פסוק says it will be raised. Someone who makes himself low like a valley is raised by הקב״ה. With this line the story ends, and the next line starts a new topic.

keyTerms.meaning: As it is said (introduces a פסוק)

phrases.english: As it is said: 'Every valley shall be lifted up.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes the story about humility from the previous section.
steps.raayaObject: Someone who humbles himself is raised up

steps.title: A vow against grain
steps.stepSummary: Someone who vows off דגן is forbidden in dry Egyptian beans but permitted in fresh ones, and permitted in rice and in split or crushed wheat.
steps.simpleTranslation: A ברייתא teaches: one who vows off grain is forbidden even in dry Egyptian beans, but permitted in fresh ones. He is also permitted in rice and in wheat that was split in two, three, or four pieces.
steps.whatsHappening: A new topic begins. The גמרא brings a ברייתא about what counts as 'grain' when someone makes a נדר against it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The rule follows how people speak. Dry beans are stored and used like grain, so people call them 'grain.' Fresh beans are eaten like a vegetable, so they are not included. Rice and crushed wheat are called by their own names, so they fall outside the word דגן.

phrases.english: It was taught: one who vows off grain —
is forbidden even in dry Egyptian beans,
and permitted in fresh ones.
And he is permitted in rice,
in wheat split in two, crushed in three, and crushed in four.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic after the story ends.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A vow against דגן covers dry beans, but not fresh beans, rice, or crushed wheat.

steps.title: A vow against produce of the year
steps.stepSummary: 'Produce of the year' covers plant foods only. 'Growths of the year' covers animals, milk, and eggs too.
steps.simpleTranslation: One who vows off produce of the year is forbidden in all that year's produce, but permitted in kids, lambs, milk, eggs, and young birds. If he said 'growths of the year are forbidden to me,' he is forbidden in all of them.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא continues with a second kind of vow, 'produce of the year,' and explains what it includes and what it leaves out.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word פירות means things that grow from plants, so animal foods are left out. The word גידולי means anything that grew or developed that year, so it includes young animals, milk, and eggs. A small change in wording changes how wide the vow is.

phrases.english: One who vows off produce of the year —
is forbidden in all produce of the year,
and permitted in young goats and lambs
and in milk, eggs, and young birds.
And if he said 'growths of the year are forbidden to me' —
he is forbidden in all of them.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the same ברייתא with another kind of vow.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: פירות השנה covers plant produce only. גידולי שנה also covers animals, milk, and eggs.

steps.title: A vow against produce of the land
steps.stepSummary: 'Produce of the land' does not include mushrooms and truffles, but 'growths of the ground' does.
steps.simpleTranslation: One who vows off produce of the land is forbidden in all produce of the land, but permitted in truffles and mushrooms. If he said 'growths of the ground are forbidden to me,' he is forbidden in all of them.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא gives a third vow, 'produce of the land.' It says mushrooms and truffles are not included unless he used the wider word 'growths.'
steps.deeperAnalysis: Mushrooms are not called 'produce of the land,' so a vow using that phrase leaves them permitted. If he says 'growths of the ground,' they are forbidden, which means they do grow from the ground in some way. This detail sets up the question in the next step.
steps.whatToRemember: The ברייתא treats mushrooms as 'growths of the ground' but not as 'produce of the land.' The rest of the section depends on this.

phrases.english: One who vows off produce of the land —
is forbidden in all produce of the land,
and permitted in truffles and mushrooms.
And if he said 'growths of the ground are forbidden to me' —
he is forbidden in all of them.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the ברייתא with a third kind of vow.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Mushrooms and truffles are left out of a vow on פירות הארץ but included in a vow on גידולי קרקע.

steps.title: Contradiction from the laws of ברכות
steps.stepSummary: The rules of ברכות say mushrooms get שהכל because they do not grow from the ground. That seems to contradict the ברייתא, which counts them as 'growths of the ground.'
steps.simpleTranslation: The גמרא sets up a contradiction: over something that does not grow from the ground, one says 'שהכל נהיה בדברו.' And a ברייתא teaches that over salt, brine, truffles, and mushrooms one says 'שהכל נהיה בדברו.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a משנה and a ברייתא from the laws of ברכות. Together they show that mushrooms are treated as not growing from the ground, which clashes with our ברייתא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה says שהכל is for things that do not grow from the ground. The ברייתא puts mushrooms on that list, so mushrooms must not grow from the ground. Our ברייתא said 'growths of the ground' includes mushrooms. Both cannot be true as they stand.

keyTerms.meaning: The ברכה 'By Whose word everything came to be'

steps.confusionAlert: Do not mix up the two sources. The first quote is from a משנה in ברכות, and the second, after וְתַנְיָא, is a ברייתא that puts mushrooms on the שהכל list.

phrases.aramaic: וּרְמִינְהִי: עַל דָּבָר שֶׁאֵין גִּידּוּלוֹ מִן הָאָרֶץ —
phrases.english: And we raise a contradiction: over something whose growth is not from the ground —
one says 'By Whose word everything came to be,'
and it was taught: over salt and over brine
and over truffles and mushrooms —
one says 'By Whose word everything came to be.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the last part of the ברייתא about mushrooms.
steps.kashyaTarget: The ברייתא's ruling that mushrooms are included in 'growths of the ground'
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברכות sources show mushrooms count as not growing from the ground, which contradicts calling them 'growths of the ground.'

steps.title: אביי: mushrooms grow from the earth but feed from the air
steps.stepSummary: אביי explains that mushrooms do grow out of the ground, but they get their food from the air, not from the soil.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said: as for growing, they grow from the earth. As for feeding, they feed from the air and not from the earth.
steps.whatsHappening: אביי answers the contradiction by splitting 'growing' from 'feeding.'
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since mushrooms come up out of the ground, a vow on 'growths of the ground' includes them. Their nourishment comes from the air, which is why they get שהכל. Each source is looking at a different part of how the mushroom lives.

phrases.english: אביי said: as for growing, they grow from the earth,
but as for feeding, they feed from the air and not from the earth.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the contradiction raised in step 5.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinction: growing from the ground versus feeding from the ground
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Mushrooms either come from the ground or they don't, so the sources clash.
steps.terutzMaskana: Mushrooms grow from the ground, so the vow includes them. They feed from the air, so their ברכה is שהכל.

steps.title: But the משנה's wording is about growth
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא pushes back: the משנה in ברכות speaks of 'growth,' not 'feeding,' so אביי's answer does not fit its words.
steps.simpleTranslation: But it teaches: 'over something whose growth is not from the ground'!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges אביי using the exact wording of the משנה in ברכות.
steps.deeperAnalysis: אביי admitted that mushrooms grow from the ground. The משנה gives שהכל only to things whose growth is not from the ground. By its plain words, mushrooms should then not get שהכל.

keyTerms.meaning: But it teaches! (a challenge from a source's wording)

phrases.english: But it teaches:
'over something whose growth is not from the ground'!

steps.kashyaTarget: אביי's distinction between growing and feeding
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The משנה ties שהכל to growth, and אביי agreed mushrooms grow from the ground, so they should not get שהכל.

steps.title: Reading the משנה as 'does not feed from the ground'
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא adjusts the wording of the משנה to say 'something that does not feed from the ground,' which fits אביי.
steps.simpleTranslation: Teach it this way: 'over something that does not feed from the ground.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers by changing the reading of the משנה so it matches אביי's explanation.
steps.deeperAnalysis: With the new reading, the rule for שהכל depends on where the food gets its nourishment, not where it sprouts. Mushrooms feed from the air, so they get שהכל, and they still count as 'growths of the ground' for vows. Both sources now agree.
steps.whatToRemember: Mushrooms grow out of the ground, so they are included in a vow on גידולי קרקע. They feed from the air, so their ברכה is שהכל. The משנה in ברכות is read as 'does not feed from the ground.'

phrases.english: Teach it this way: over something
that does not feed from the ground.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in step 7 by changing the wording of the משנה.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Changing the reading of the source text
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The משנה makes the ברכה depend on where a food grows.
steps.terutzMaskana: The משנה makes the ברכה depend on where a food feeds, which matches אביי.

steps.title: Vowing off clothing, wool, or flax
steps.stepSummary: The משנה rules that a vow against clothing does not include sackcloth, sheets, or coarse curtains, and a vow against wool or flax does not include raw fleece or raw flax.
steps.simpleTranslation: Someone who vows off clothing may still use sackcloth, a sheet, or a coarse curtain. If he said 'Wool is קונם on me,' he may cover himself with raw wool fleece. If he said 'Flax is on me,' he may cover himself with bundles of raw flax.
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה begins. It defines what the word 'clothing' covers in a vow, and what 'wool' and 'flax' cover.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A vow follows how people normally talk. People do not call sackcloth or a sheet 'clothing,' and when they say 'wool' they mean wool fabric, not raw fleece. So these items stay permitted.

keyTerms.meaning: A vow word meaning 'forbidden to me like a קרבן'
Raw wool fleece, not yet made into cloth
A coarse, rough curtain or cloth

phrases.english: MISHNA
One who vows off clothing
is permitted in sackcloth, in a sheet, and in a coarse curtain.
If he said: "Wool is קונם, I will not put it on myself"
he is permitted to cover himself with raw wool fleece.
If he said: "Flax, I will not put it on myself"
he is permitted to cover himself with bundles of raw flax.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new משנה on a new subject: vows about clothing.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A vow against clothing, wool, or flax covers only what people normally call by that name, so sackcloth, sheets, raw fleece, and raw flax stay permitted.

steps.title: רבי יהודה: everything follows the person's intent
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהודה says a vow follows what the person meant. A man who sweated while carrying wool and linen may still wear them, but may not carry them on his back.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יהודה says: everything depends on the one who vows. If he was carrying wool and linen, sweated, and they smelled bad, and he said 'Wool and linen are קונם on me,' he may still wear them, but he may not sling them over his back.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יהודה adds a new rule to the משנה: look at the situation to understand what the person meant by his vow.
steps.deeperAnalysis: His words sound like a vow against wearing, but the situation shows he was upset about carrying. So the vow forbids carrying the bundle and leaves wearing permitted.

keyTerms.meaning: Everything follows the intent of the one who vows
To sling something over his back as a load

steps.whyThisMatters: This shows that the situation around a vow can decide its meaning, even more than the exact words.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yehuda says,
Everything is according to the one who vows:
If he was carrying a load and sweated,
and its smell was bad,
and he said: "Wool and linen are קונם, I will not put them on myself"
he is permitted to cover himself with them,
but he is forbidden to sling them over his back.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי יְהוּדָה אוֹמֵר, הַכֹּל לְפִי הַנּוֹדֵר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a second view to the משנה, focusing on the vower's intent rather than the normal meaning of words.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A vow is read according to the vower's situation and intent; here it forbids carrying wool and linen, not wearing them.

steps.title: A ברייתא lists items that do count as clothing
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes a ברייתא that repeats the permitted items and adds a list of forbidden items, such as belts, aprons, socks, trousers, and a hat.
steps.simpleTranslation: A ברייתא teaches: Someone who vows off clothing may use sackcloth, a sheet, and a coarse curtain. But he may not use a money belt, a sash, a סקורטיא, a leather spread, a leather sock, a leather apron, trousers, or a hat.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins by quoting a ברייתא that adds to the משנה. It lists items that the vow does include.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה only told us what is permitted. The ברייתא adds the other side: smaller items worn on the body, like belts, aprons, and hats, are called clothing, so the vow includes them.

phrases.english: GEMARA
It was taught in a ברייתא: One who vows off clothing
is permitted in sackcloth, a sheet, and a coarse curtain,
but forbidden in a money belt and a sash,
and a סקורטיא and a leather spread,
phrases.notes: The גמרא explains סקורטיא in the next two lines.

phrases.english: and a leather sock and a leather apron,
and trousers and a hat.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Expands the משנה's first ruling by listing what the vow does forbid.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Belts, sashes, aprons, leather socks, trousers, and hats count as clothing for this vow.

steps.title: What is an איסקורטי?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what one unfamiliar item in the ברייתא's list is.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא stops to ask the meaning of a hard word from the ברייתא. This sets up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is not a challenge. The גמרא just wants to know which item is meant, so we know what the vow includes.

keyTerms.meaning: An item of clothing from the list (called סקורטיא above)

phrases.english: What is "איסקורטי"?
phrases.notes: This is the same item the ברייתא called סקורטיא, just spelled a bit differently.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks about a word from the ברייתא just quoted.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The meaning of the word איסקורטי (סקורטיא) in the ברייתא.

steps.title: רבה בר חנה: a tanner's apron
steps.stepSummary: רבה בר חנה explains that the item is a tanner's leather apron.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבה בר חנה said: It is a tanner's apron.
steps.whatsHappening: רבה בר חנה answers the question: the word means the apron a tanner wears.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A tanner's apron is worn on the body while working, so it counts as clothing, and the vow includes it.

keyTerms.meaning: A tanner's garment, a leather apron

phrases.english: Rabba bar Chana said:
A tanner's apron.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבָּה בַּר חָנָה: כִּיתּוּנָא דְצַלָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question about the word איסקורטי.

steps.title: Going out on שבת in rain coverings
steps.stepSummary: A second ברייתא teaches that on שבת a person may go out wearing thick sackcloth, a thick blanket, a sheet, or a coarse curtain against the rain, but not a box, basket, or mat.
steps.simpleTranslation: A ברייתא teaches: One may go out in thick sackcloth, a thick blanket, a sheet, or a coarse curtain because of the rain. But not in a box, a basket, or a mat because of the rain.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes another ברייתא that talks about the same kinds of items: sackcloth, sheets, and coarse curtains. This time the topic is going out on שבת.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Things a person wraps around his body to stay dry may be worn out on שבת. A box, basket, or mat is not worn; it is just held over the head, so it may not be taken out.

keyTerms.meaning: One may go out (into a public area on שבת)

steps.confusionAlert: Do not confuse the two topics. The משנה said sackcloth is not 'clothing' in how people speak about vows. This ברייתא is about שבת, where sackcloth worn against the rain may be worn out. These are two different questions.

phrases.english: It was taught in a ברייתא: One may go out in thick sackcloth
phrases.notes: He means going out into a public area on שבת.

phrases.english: and in a thick wool blanket,
and in a sheet and a coarse curtain, because of the rain,
but not in a box and not in a basket,
and not in a mat, because of the rain.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings a related ברייתא that deals with the same items (sackcloth, sheet, coarse curtain) in the setting of שבת.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: On שבת one may go out wrapped in sackcloth, a blanket, a sheet, or a coarse curtain against rain, but not under a box, basket, or mat.

steps.title: Shepherds, and everyone else too
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא adds that shepherds may go out in sackcloth, and explains that this applies to everyone; חכמים just mentioned shepherds because they usually wear it.
steps.simpleTranslation: Shepherds may go out in sackcloth. And they did not say this only about shepherds, but about every person. חכמים simply spoke about what usually happens.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא finishes by mentioning shepherds, and then makes clear the rule is for everyone.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Someone might think only shepherds may go out in sackcloth. The ברייתא says no: shepherds were named only because they usually dress that way, but anyone may.

keyTerms.meaning: חכמים spoke about the common, usual case

steps.whatToRemember: A vow against 'clothing' follows how people talk, so sackcloth is not included. רבי יהודה adds that the vower's situation decides. For שבת, coverings wrapped on the body against rain may be worn out, and when חכמים name a group, like shepherds, they are often just describing the usual case.
steps.whyThisMatters: The idea 'דברו חכמים בהווה' is a rule used all over ש״ס: an example in a ruling does not always limit the ruling to that case.

phrases.english: Shepherds may go out in sackcloth.
And they did not say this only about shepherds,
but about every person,
only that the Sages spoke about the usual case.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְלֹא רוֹעִים בִּלְבַד אָמְרוּ, אֶלָּא כׇּל אָדָם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes the second ברייתא and makes its rule general.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Anyone, not only shepherds, may go out on שבת in sackcloth; shepherds were mentioned only because חכמים spoke about the usual case.

steps.title: Quoting רבי יהודה's view from the משנה
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes רבי יהודה's line from the משנה, that everything depends on the one who vows, so it can explain it.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יהודה says: everything follows the one who vows, and so on.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings back a line from our משנה, רבי יהודה's opinion, to start discussing it. This is a setup line for the next move.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the משנה, רבי יהודה said a vow is understood according to the person making it. That idea is still general and unclear. The גמרא quotes it now so the ברייתא that follows can show what it means in practice.

keyTerms.meaning: Everything follows the one who vows; the vow's meaning depends on his situation and intent

phrases.english: Rabbi Yehuda says:
Everything is according to the one who vows, etc.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי יְהוּדָה אוֹמֵר הַכֹּל לְפִי הַנּוֹדֵר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the ברייתות about wearing clothes on שבת and goes back to a new line in the משנה
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבי יהודה holds that a vow is understood according to the vower's situation and intent.

steps.title: The ברייתא asks how רבי יהודה's rule works
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא asks what kind of case רבי יהודה meant when he said everything follows the one who vows.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was taught in a ברייתא: How did רבי יהודה mean 'everything follows the one who vows'?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא that opens with a question about רבי יהודה's rule. It is setting up the examples that come next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'Everything follows the vower' is too general to apply on its own. The ברייתא asks for a concrete case, so we can see how the person's situation changes what his words mean.

phrases.english: It is taught: How did Rabbi Yehuda say
'Everything is according to the one who vows'?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for practical examples of the rule quoted in step 16
steps.sheelahInformationSought: In what kind of case does the vower's situation decide what his vow means?

steps.title: Wool: the vow forbids only wearing it
steps.stepSummary: Someone who is uncomfortable wearing wool and vows 'wool shall not come upon me' may not wear wool, but he may carry it.
steps.simpleTranslation: If he was wearing wool, it bothered him, and he said 'Wool is קונם, it shall not come upon me,' he may not wear wool but he may carry it.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא gives its first example. The discomfort came from wearing wool, so the vow is read as being about wearing it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The words 'come upon me' could mean wearing or carrying. Because the vow came out of the discomfort of wearing wool, only wearing is forbidden. Carrying a load of wool is still allowed.

keyTerms.meaning: A word used to make a vow, meaning 'forbidden to me like a קרבן'
Comes upon me; the vow's wording, which can mean wearing or carrying
It bothered him, it made him uncomfortable

phrases.english: If he was wearing wool and it bothered him,
and he said, 'Wool is konam, it shall not come upon me,'
he is forbidden to wear it but permitted to carry it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the first answer to the ברייתא's question in step 17
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: When the vow came from discomfort while wearing wool, it forbids only wearing wool, not carrying it.

steps.title: Flax: the vow forbids only carrying it
steps.stepSummary: Someone who sweats while carrying flax and vows 'flax shall not come upon me' may still wear flax, but he may not carry it.
steps.simpleTranslation: If he was carrying flax, began sweating, and said 'Flax is קונם, it shall not come upon me,' he may wear flax but he may not carry it.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא gives a second example that is the reverse of the first. Here the trouble came from carrying, so the vow is about carrying.
steps.deeperAnalysis: These are the same words as in the wool case, but the result is the opposite. The sweating came from the load, so carrying flax is forbidden and wearing flax clothes stays permitted. This shows רבי יהודה's rule clearly: the situation decides what the words mean.
steps.whatToRemember: For רבי יהודה, the same vow, 'it shall not come upon me,' means 'wearing' if wearing caused the trouble and 'carrying' if carrying caused it. The vower's situation decides what he meant.
steps.confusionAlert: Don't think wool is always about wearing and flax is always about carrying. The material is not what matters. What matters is what the person was doing when he made the vow.

phrases.english: If he was carrying flax and was sweating,
and he said, 'Flax is konam, it shall not come upon me,'
he is permitted to wear it but forbidden to carry it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the matching reverse case to step 18, completing the ברייתא's answer
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: When the vow came from sweating while carrying flax, it forbids only carrying flax, not wearing it.
steps.whyThisMatters: Putting the two cases side by side shows that רבי יהודה reads a vow by the vower's circumstances, not only by the plain meaning of his words.
